newsitem.title: USA: Philadelphia musicians take up picket signs.
newsitem.headline: Philadelphia musicians take up picket signs.

text.p: Striking musicians of the Philadelphia Orchestra set up picket lines on Monday forcing the cancellation of the season's opening night gala.

The 103 musicians and two librarians, members of the American Federation of Musicians, voted on Friday to reject the orchestra's final offer and voted 100-0 on Sunday to conduct their first strike in 30 years.

Bob Bedard, a spokesman for the musicians, said "management has already called to seek resumption of negotiations," but he did not predict a quick end to the strike. "We are still far apart," he said.

As pickets went up at the Academy of Music, orchestra management cancelled the opening night of the 1996-97 season planned for Tuesday and the rest of its schedule to Sept. 24. It told patrons to trade in their tickets for cash or hold them to use at a future concert. Subscribers for the full season were asked to consider donating their ticket prices.

A key issue in the dispute is a request for a $6,000 annual "electronic media guarantee," a share of the orchestra's income from radio performances and recordings. The orchestra has neither a recording contract nor regular broadcasts.

The last management offer included a 10 percent raise in the $72,000 base salary over three years and a one-year electronic media guarantee of $2,000, orchestra board chairman Peter Benoliel said. It also includes a health coverage copayment that by the end of the contract will be a maximum of $40 a week.
"The strike is regrettable. It doesn't benefit the musicians. It doesn't benefit the orchestra, and it doesn't benefit the community," Benoliel said.
"This is not about money," Bedard said. "The musicians are asking the orchestra to protect its own future."
Musicians will begin collecting $150 weekly strike benefits from their union.
